absent: Numeric signal range and kernel-only signal set beyond validation behavior.
Platform-specific adjustments performed by alternate stack size validation and compat ABI hook.
Internals of pending-queue flushing, mask helpers, timer re-arm, and current-mask publication.
Scheduler sleep and wakeup mechanics behind suspension and pending detection.
User ABI numeric values for flags, modes, error codes, permissions and size constants.
Ownership and lifetime of handler restorer fields across architectures.
Cross-call enqueue, interrupt delivery, callback execution context and timeout enforcement.
Sysctl registration effects and slab cache allocation failure modes.

findings.text: A central installer publishes a new disposition for the calling thread group and optionally returns the prior disposition. Acceptance depends on a valid regular signal and a mutable slot. Visible effects include normalization of flag bits through a platform hook and coherent update of handler and mask.

Disposition change rejects kernel-reserved signals when a new action is supplied, rejects immutable slots, clears flag bits outside the user ABI subset on both new and returned actions, and never retains termination or stop signals in a handler mask.

The signal handler exclusion with interrupt suppression protects inspection and publication of the disposition table across the whole update including compat adjustment and queue maintenance. One alternate-stack build uses the same exclusion while the other build uses no locking.

When the resulting disposition ignores the signal, queued instances are discarded from shared state and from every thread of the group regardless of blocking. A transition away from ignored re-enables timer-related handling for that signal.

Alternate stack management supports independent query and update. Query reports pointer, size and combined flags. An update that changes nothing succeeds without locking. Disable clears identity while enable enforces a minimum size and platform size validity.

Alternate stack update is refused while execution is already on that stack. Undersized requests fail with a memory-size status. Identical state avoids side effects. Native and compat paths use different minimum size requirements and different stack pointer sources.

Native and compat alternate stack services copy user argument blocks, delegate to shared logic, and copy back prior state where requested. Restore helpers report user memory faults but suppress other failures. Save helpers publish current task pointer, size and flags to user memory.
Alternate stack mode accepts only disabled, on-stack and zero values apart from preserved flag bits. Separate native and compat minimum stack size constants govern enablement.

Disposition install and query is exposed through modern wide-mask, legacy narrow-mask and compat forms. Each validates user buffers and expected mask width, translates narrow masks or compat pointers where needed, shares one core installer, and reports user memory faults distinctly from validation failures.

Mask and pending inspection includes narrow current-mask read, narrow mask replacement returning its predecessor, a three-mode narrow block operation, and pending-set retrieval with a user width check plus a compat form returning the low word.
Mask update modes are block, unblock and set-mask. Simple handler installation uses one-shot semantics with no additional blocked signals during handling.
A simple signal service installs a handler with empty mask and one-shot no-mask flags, then returns the previous handler on success.

Suspension waits interruptibly until a signal is pending for the caller. A temporary mask can be installed for the wait with the prior mask saved for restoration on return. Both pause-like and suspend-like waits exit with a restart-without-handler status.

Native and kernel signal information views must agree in total size and in offsets for process identity, timer, realtime, child, fault, poll and system-call payloads. Identity and address views alias, with word-size dependent layout rules, and compat identity fields have their own width and offset rules.
A weakly provided region naming hook reports no name by default and may be overridden by platform code.

Two control tables expose a fatal-signal printing toggle and an optional exception tracing toggle as integer vectors with owner-write and world-read permissions, registered under separate namespaces during early initialization.
Early signal initialization first validates signal information layout compatibility, then creates an accounted slab cache for queued signal nodes with panic behavior on allocation failure.

Debugger-requested delivery uses a non-blocking attempt on handler exclusion and informs the operator on contention. Delivery to a non-running target is refused on first request for a new target to avoid run-queue deadlock, with a repeat for the same target treated as explicit risk acceptance.
Cross-call per-processor state bundles per-processor call descriptors with two processor masks, one for targeting and one for interrupt delivery.

Cross-call processor state is prepared by allocating node-local masks and lazily allocating descriptor storage that is retained across offline periods for lock waiters. Teardown frees the masks. The dying phase drains pending callbacks and runs deferred work while interrupts are suppressed.

The cross-call queue drain requires suppressed interrupts, re-enables backtrace requests, detaches and reverses the whole queue, warns once about work sent to offline processors, completes synchronous waiters before asynchronous and interrupt-work items, and finally batches pending wakeups together.
Queue draining asserts interrupts are suppressed on entry, establishing an interrupt-free critical section for detaching and completing cross-call work on the local processor.
Early cross-call initialization prepares per-processor queues for every possible processor and prepares the boot processor control state.

Call-descriptor lock diagnostics keep per-processor current descriptor plus captured callback and argument, a millisecond stall threshold with a default value, an optional panic threshold, a per-processor backtrace gate, and global counters for observed faults and stuck locks.
A boot option controls descriptor-lock debugging by parsing an unsigned value and enabling or disabling a static branch accordingly.
This translation unit prefixes diagnostic messages with its module name and instantiates its tracepoints locally.
